hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 1. All had contributed to the decline and eventual downfall of Aksum, except: (2015)

options.text: A. Internal rebellions from the Beja, the Agaw & Queen Bani al Hamwiyah (Yodit)
B. Succession problems and power struggle within the ruling families
C. The rise and expansion of the Muslim Arabs

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The decline of the Aksumite Empire was primarily driven by environmental degradation, the loss of Red Sea trade routes due to the rise of Muslim Arabs, and internal rebellions from subject groups like the Beja and Agaw (notably under Queen Yodit). Succession problems and power struggles are not cited as a primary historical cause for Aksum's specific downfall, making it the exception.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 2. Which of the following is incorrect about the Zagwe period (1150-1270) (2015)

options.text: A. It was the golden age in painting and construction of rock-hew churches
B. Succession problems & oppositions from their opponents accounted for their downfall
C. Its rulers were detached from the previous Aksumite tradition & culture
D. Their opponents accused them as 'usurpers' or 'illegitimate'
E. Its political center was Adafa, near Roha/Lalibela

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Zagwe rulers were not detached from previous Aksumite traditions; they heavily continued and preserved Aksumite religious, architectural, and cultural practices, including Orthodox Christianity and the tradition of church building. The claim that they were detached is historically incorrect.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 3. Which one is NOT true about the Muslim sultanates in Ethiopia & the Horn? (2015)

options.text: A. Their rulers exercised both political and religious power
B. Many of them were located along the Zeila trade routes
C. They were formed mainly because of Islam and trade
D. The rivalry to control the trade was the root cause for their conflict with the Christian Kingdom
E. Until the early 16th century they had an upper hand over the Christian Kingdom

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Until the early 16th century (specifically the rise of Ahmad Gragn), the Christian Kingdom generally maintained military and political dominance over the Muslim sultanates, notably during the reigns of strong emperors like Amda Seyon and Zara Yaqob. The Muslim sultanates did not have the upper hand prior to this period.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 4. The royal prison of Amba Gishen (2015)

options.text: A. was established by Yekuno-Amlak to resolve succession problems
B. made all the male successors to be confined in solitary place
C. was destroyed by the forces of Emir Nur Mujahid in 1557
D. it further intensified succession problems among the ruling families

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Amba Gishen was used as a royal prison where all male members of the Solomonic dynasty (except the ruling emperor) were confined to prevent succession disputes and civil wars. It was actually established by Yagbe'a Seyon (not Yekuno-Amlak) and was captured by Ahmad Gragn in 1540 (not Emir Nur in 1557).

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 5. All are the reforms of Zara-Yaqob (r. 1434-68) except: (2015)

options.text: A. made lasting peace with the Estifanosites by reviving Sabbath
B. encouraged the establishment of a library in every church
C. insisted the clergy to preach Christianity in remote areas
D. ordered the people to observe fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Emperor Zara Yaqob did not make peace with the Estifanosites (Stephanites); rather, he harshly persecuted them for their refusal to bow to the Cross and the Virgin Mary, leading to severe punishments and executions. He did, however, mandate the observance of the Sabbath, fasting, and church libraries.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 6. Which one of the following is incorrect about the Sultanate of Ifat? (2015)

options.text: A. it weakened and incorporated the Sultanate of Shewa
B. it was founded by Umar Walasma who claimed descent from the Hashamite clan of Arabia
C. around 1367 its rulers moved to eastern lowlands & formed the sultanate of Adal
D. in 1576 its rulers shifted their capital from Dakar to Harar
E. the first conflict with the Christian Kingdom broke out after Haqaddin I jailed Ti'iyintay

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The shift of the capital from Dakar to Harar occurred under the Sultanate of Adal, not Ifat. The Sultanate of Ifat had already been extinguished and succeeded by Adal long before 1576.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 7. In which of the following battlefields the forces of Adal faced defeat in 1543? (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The forces of Adal, led by Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (Gragn), were decisively defeated at the Battle of Woyna Dega in 1543. Ahmad Gragn was killed during this battle by a joint force of Ethiopians and Portuguese musketeers.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 8. The following rulers of Adal lost their life while fighting the Christian Kingdom, except: (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Emir Nur Mujahid of Harar did not die in battle against the Christian Kingdom. While he fought and killed Emperor Gelawdewos in 1559, Emir Nur himself died of sickness (likely famine or disease) in Harar in 1567.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 7. Which one of the following was a major cause for the 16th century war between the Christian and Muslim sultanates? (2015)

options.text: A. the desire to control the lucrative trade & trade routes
B. population pressure caused by push and pull factors
D. the intervention of foreign powers

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: While religion served as an ideological rallying point, the primary underlying root cause of the conflict between the Christian Kingdom and the Muslim sultanates in the 16th century was economic: specifically, the desire to control the lucrative Zeila trade route.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 8. All of these Christian emperors lost their life while fighting against Adal, except: (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Emperor Sarsa-Dengil died of a sudden illness in 1597 while campaigning against the Beta Israel, not in battle against the Sultanate of Adal. Emperors Yishaq, Tewodros I, and Gelawdewos all fell in battle against Muslim forces.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 9. All are the consequences of the war between the Christian Kingdom & Adal, except: (2015)

options.text: A. heavy human loss and material damage
B. intermingling & cultural interactions among various ethnic groups
C. exhausted both states and made them an easy prey for the advancing Oromos
D. it helped the revival of monarchial power
E. Opened the room for the Jesuit interlude in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The 16th-century wars severely weakened and exhausted the central authority of both the Christian Kingdom and the Sultanate of Adal. It did not help revive monarchical power; rather, it initiated a long period of instability and decentralization.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 10. All are true about the Emirate of Harar except: (2015)

options.text: A. it was occupied by the Egyptians from 1875 to 1885
B. Emir Nur Mujahid made it a walled city
C. in the mid-17 century Emir Ali ibn-Da'ud established a new dynasty
D. it was one of the major centers of Islamic power and culture in the region
E. peacefully submitted to the forces of Shewa in 1887

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Emirate of Harar did not peacefully submit to Shewa. It was forcibly incorporated into the Ethiopian empire after the forces of Emir Abdullahi were defeated by Menelik II at the Battle of Chelenqo in January 1887.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 11. Which of the following is incorrect about the gadaa system? (2015)

options.text: A. it constituted elements of democracy like periodic succession & power
B. it was a means of socialization, education, maintaining peace & order, and social cohesion
C. it resembled with the monarchial institution as it is based on hereditary rule
D. it was apparently practiced by the Oromos long before their movement in the 16th century
E. the senior Qallu/Abba Muda played pivotal role in power transfer & legitimizing the gadaa

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Gadaa system is inherently an egalitarian, age-grade democratic socio-political structure with periodic, elected transfers of power every eight years. It is fundamentally opposite to a hereditary monarchical institution.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 12. Who was the immediate successor of Emperor Tewodros II: (2015)

options.text: A. Ras Adal Tesema of Gojjam
B. Dejjach Kassa Mircha of Tigray

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Following the death of Emperor Tewodros II in 1868 at Maqdala, Wagshum Gobeze of Lasta proclaimed himself emperor, taking the throne name Tekle Giyorgis II. He was later defeated by Kassa Mircha (who became Yohannes IV).

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 13. Select the wrong pair: (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Kasa Mircha was crowned as Emperor Yohannes IV, not Yohannes II. Yohannes II was an earlier monarch who ruled briefly during the Zemene Mesafint.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 14. All are true about the 1884 Adwa or Hewett Treaty, except: (2015)

options.text: A. It was signed between Yohnnes IV & the British on behalf of Egypt
B. It resulted in animosity and conflict between Ethiopia and the Mahadists
C. Restored the port of Massawa as free port to Yohannes IV
D. Enabled the safe evacuation of the trapped Egyptian soldiers through Ethiopian territories
E. Brought the Italians to Massawa who began encroaching the hinterland

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Hewett (Adwa) Treaty of 1884 did not bring the Italians to Massawa; rather, the British secretly encouraged Italy to occupy Massawa in 1885 in violation of the treaty's spirit, to prevent the French from taking it. The treaty itself promised Ethiopia free transit via the port.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 15. The term of the office of Abba Gadaa lasts for (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: In the traditional Oromo Gadaa system, power is held by a designated generation set for a strictly defined period of eight years before peacefully transferring to the next generation set.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 16. Before its incorporation in 1894, the Chiefs/Kings of Walayta used a title : (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The political leaders or kings of the Walayta kingdom used the royal title 'Kawo'. ('Tato' was used in Kafa, and 'Mekericho' refers to a council of advisors.)

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 17. Which one of the following is NOT related to the legacy of the victory of Adwa (2015)

options.text: A. made Ethiopia the only independent & sovereign African state
B. it is considered as one of the remarkable black victories over the white colonizers
C. it motivated other colonial people to fight for their independence
D. led the country to endless civil war and political instability
E. made Ethiopia a symbol of anti-colonial movement

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Battle of Adwa (1896) actually consolidated the Ethiopian Empire and solidified Emperor Menelik II's internal power and international recognition. It did not lead to endless civil war and instability; rather, it brought a period of relative peace and modernization.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 18. Which one of the following did not belong to the attempted reforms of Tewodros II? (2015)

options.text: A. The abolition of slave trade
C. Arms factory and ministerial system
D. Land reform and banning polygamy

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: While Emperor Tewodros II did attempt to establish an arms factory (at Gafat) and a salaried national army, the creation of a 'ministerial system' was a much later reform introduced by Emperor Menelik II in 1907. Thus, the pairing in option C is incorrect regarding Tewodros's reforms.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 19. The Borumeda Council (1878) (2015)

options.text: A. presided by Yohannes IV to bring religious unity and uniformity
B. brought the end of the power struggle between two vassal kings of Shewa & Gojjam
C. passed strong resolution to check the expansion of Egyptians and Mahadists
D. made the first attempt to introduce religious freedom and abolish slave trade
E. resulted in peaceful conversion of Muslims to Orthodox Christianity

hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Council of Boru Meda (1878) was convened by Emperor Yohannes IV primarily to settle theological disputes within the Ethiopian Orthodox Church (e.g., Qibat vs. Tewahedo) and mandate religious uniformity, which included forcing the Muslims of Wollo to convert to Christianity.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 20. Which of the following items served as medium of exchange in the 19th c long distance trade? (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Both Amole (salt bars) and the Maria Theresa Thaler (silver coin) served as the primary media of exchange in Ethiopian 19th-century long-distance trade. Amole was used for smaller domestic transactions, while the Thaler was the standard currency for major and international trade.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 1. The Neolithic Revolution was well noted for transforming the life of Ancient Society (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Neolithic Revolution marked a profound turning point in human history characterized by the transition from nomadic hunting and gathering to settled agriculture and the domestication of animals, thereby radically transforming ancient societal structures.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 2. Gult was a right to administer and collect tribute on rist owners' produce (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: In the traditional Ethiopian land tenure system, Gult was a fief right granted by the monarch to the nobility or the church, enabling them to administer regions and collect tribute and labor from the peasants (Rist owners) who lived and farmed there.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 3. Trade was not only a source of conflict but also a means of social cohesion and integration. (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: While competition over trade routes often led to major conflicts (such as the Adal-Christian wars), markets and long-distance trade networks also heavily fostered cultural exchange, intermarriage, linguistic spread, and peaceful interdependence among diverse ethnic groups in the Horn of Africa.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 4. Once history is written there is no room for new historical reinterpretation. (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: History is a dynamic and evolving discipline. Historical reinterpretation, or historiographical revisionism, continually occurs as new primary sources are discovered, marginalized perspectives are brought to light, and new analytical methods are applied.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 5. The Turks & the Mahadists intervened in the conflict between the Christian Kingdom & Adal. (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: While the Ottoman Turks did actively support the Adal Sultanate during the 16th-century conflicts (providing firearms and mercenaries), the Mahdists were a 19th-century Sudanese movement and had no involvement in the 16th-century Adal-Christian war.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 6. The Jesuit intervention caused a bloody civil war & religious controversy in the Christian Kingdom (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The aggressive proselytization by Jesuit missionaries, leading to Emperor Susenyos officially converting to Catholicism in 1622, triggered widespread rebellions and a devastating religious civil war within the Ethiopian Orthodox population, forcing his abdication in 1632.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 7. In the 14th century Christian Kingdom a king who started rapid and large scale territorial expansion is noted for undertaking major religious reforms (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: This statement conflates two distinct monarchs. Emperor Amda Seyon (r. 1314–1344) is the 14th-century ruler famous for rapid territorial expansion, but the noted major religious reforms (such as enforcing Sabbath observance) were primarily undertaken by Emperor Zara Yaqob in the 15th century (r. 1434–1468).

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text:
Part III: Arrange the following historical events in chronological order from the earliest to the recent by using the numbers from 1 to 7
1. The first arrival of the Jesuit missionaries under Andreas de Ovideo
2. The Battle of Embabo
3. The establishment of Leqa-Naqamte by Bakare Godana
4. The Italian occupation of Massawa
5. The end of the Yejju Dynasty
6. The beginning of the Zemene Mesafint
7. The Battle of Debarqi (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Chronologically: 1. Jesuit missionaries arrived in 1557. 6. Zemene Mesafint began in 1769 with Iyoas's assassination. 3. Leqa-Naqamte was established by Bakare Godana circa 1840. 7. The Battle of Debarqi took place in 1848. 5. The end of the Yejju Dynasty was marked by the Battle of Ayshal in 1853. 2. The Battle of Embabo occurred in 1882. 4. Italian occupation of Massawa happened in 1885.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 1. Write any three characteristics of the Zemene Mesafint (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.answer: 1. The absence of a strong, effective central monarchical power; 2. Constant civil wars and destructive power struggles among regional warlords; 3. Economic stagnation, disruption of trade routes, and widespread devastation of peasant lands.
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Zemene Mesafint (Era of the Princes, 1769–1855) was a period defined by extreme decentralization. The Solomonic emperors in Gondar were reduced to mere figureheads, while regional lords continuously fought for control, causing immense socio-economic decline.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 2. The Oromo integrated non-Oromo through two adoption mechanisms namely __________ and __________ (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.answer: Guddifacha and Moggasa | Gudifacha and Mogasa
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: The Oromo utilized two main assimilation systems during their expansions: Guddifacha (the adoption of a child or youth into an Oromo family) and Moggasa (the mass adoption of a conquered community or group into an Oromo clan), granting them equal rights and obligations.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 3. The two remarkable women who took part during the war between Adal & the Christian Kingdom were __________ & __________ respectively. (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.answer: Bati Del Wambara and Seble Wongel | Bati Del Wombera and Seble Wengel
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Bati Del Wambara was the influential wife of Imam Ahmad Gragn, who rallied Adal forces and organized revenge campaigns. Empress Seble Wongel, wife of Lebna Dengel, played a crucial role in hiding in mountain fortresses and later coordinating with the Portuguese forces to defeat Adal.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 4. The three foreign powers who threatened Ethiopia's sovereignty during the reign of Yohannes IV were __________, __________ and __________. (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.answer: Egyptians, Mahdists, and Italians | Egypt, Mahdist Sudan, and Italy
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Emperor Yohannes IV faced a war on multiple fronts against distinct external invaders: Khedivate Egypt (defeated at Gundet and Gura), the Mahdist State of Sudan (whom he fought and died against at Metemma), and colonial Italy (which began encroaching from Massawa).

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 5. Write any three of the measures taken by Fasiledes after his accession to power. (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.answer: 1. He expelled the Jesuit missionaries and completely severed diplomatic ties with Rome. 2. He restored the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church as the official state religion. 3. He initiated a 'closed-door policy', isolating Ethiopia from European influence. 4. He established a permanent capital at Gondar in 1636.
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: Following the disastrous civil wars caused by his father Susenyos's conversion to Catholicism, Emperor Fasiledes systematically dismantled Catholic influence, restored the traditional church, and isolated the empire from Europe to preserve national unity and sovereignty.

hist_ASTU_2015.subject: History
hist_ASTU_2015.text: 6. As the northern Muslim merchants were called __________; __________ were the Muslim Oromo merchants of southwestern region; while __________ were the Sudanese merchants. (2015)
hist_ASTU_2015.answer: Jabarti; Afkala; Jallaba | Jeberti; Afaqala; Jellaba
hist_ASTU_2015.explanation: In 19th century long-distance trade, the 'Jabarti' (or Jeberti) were the established northern Ethiopian Muslim traders, the 'Afkala' were the Oromo Muslim merchants facilitating trade in the southwest, and the 'Jallaba' were the traders hailing from neighboring Sudan.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 1. The claim for legitimacy of the restored "Solomonic" dynasty based on legendary blood descent from King Solomon of Israel. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The Kebra Nagast was used to legitimize the restored Solomonic dynasty by claiming an unbroken lineage from King Solomon of Israel and the Queen of Sheba, framing the preceding Zagwe dynasty as illegitimate interlopers.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 2. Religion was the fundamental cause for the conflict of the Solomonic rulers with Muslim sultanates between the 13th to the 16th centuries. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: While the conflicts were often masked in religious terms, the fundamental and primary cause was economic—specifically, the struggle to control the lucrative trade routes leading to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 3. Trade was a major factor both for the rise of Muslim Sultanates and their cooperation with Christian rulers. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Trade was indeed a major factor in the rise of the Muslim Sultanates, but it primarily led to intense rivalry and conflict with Christian rulers over the control of trade routes, rather than cooperation.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 4. The external relations of medieval Ethiopian Christian kingdom with Europe were strongly influenced by the legend of "Prester John". (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The legend of Prester John—a mythical wealthy Christian king believed to reside in the East or Africa—greatly motivated European powers (especially Portugal) to seek alliances with Ethiopia against expanding Muslim powers.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 5. The battle of Shimbra Kure was fought between the armies of Made Tsiyon and Ahmad Gragn in 1529. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The Battle of Shimbra Kure in 1529 was fought between Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (Ahmad Gragn) and Emperor Libne Dingil, not Amda Tsiyon (who ruled in the 14th century).

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 6. Punt was the earliest recorded state in northern Ethiopia. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Da'amat is considered the earliest recorded state specifically located in northern Ethiopia. The Land of Punt was an ancient kingdom whose exact location is debated but generally thought to encompass the broader Horn of Africa.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 7. Emperor Susenyos was converted Catholicism to secure arms to defeat Ahmad Gragn. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Ahmad Gragn was defeated much earlier in 1543 by Emperor Gelawdewos. Emperor Susenyos converted to Catholicism in 1622 to secure an alliance with Portugal to consolidate his power against internal rebellions.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 8. The Oromo population movement of the 16th and 17th centuries resulted in exchanges of culture and languages between the Oromo their neighbours. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The widespread movement of the Oromo led to significant cultural, linguistic, and demographic intermingling, fundamentally shaping the modern cultural landscape of Ethiopia.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 9. The teaching of Ewostatewos was the strict observance of Sabbath on Saturday. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The Ewostatewos movement within the Ethiopian Orthodox Church strongly advocated for the dual observance of the Sabbath, strictly observing both Saturday and Sunday, which led to a major theological controversy.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 10. The Oromo integrated non-Oromos through Gudiffacha and Mogassa. (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Gudifacha (adoption of children) and Mogasa (adoption of individuals or groups into a clan) were traditional Oromo institutions that successfully assimilated non-Oromo populations into Oromo society.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 1. Elleni (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Empress Eleni played a powerful political role and served as regent for the young Emperor Libne Dingil during a critical period in Ethiopian medieval history.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 2. Libne Dingil (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Emperor Libne Dingil commanded the Christian forces that suffered a catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Shimbra Kure in 1529 against Imam Ahmad Gragn.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 3. Bati Del Wanbera (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Bati Del Wanbera was the influential wife of Imam Ahmad Gragn. She encouraged his military campaigns largely to avenge the death of her father, Emir Mahfuz.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 4. Ze Dingil (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Emperor Za Dengel secretly converted to Catholicism in 1603 under the influence of Jesuit missionary Pedro Paez, which eventually led to his downfall.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 5. Seble-Wongel (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Queen Mother Seble Wongel played a crucial role in advising her son, Emperor Gelawdewos, including the decisive Battle of Wayna Daga where Ahmad Gragn was finally defeated.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 6. Gelawdewos (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Emperor Gelawdewos, after defeating Ahmad Gragn, was later killed in battle in 1559 against the forces of the Adal Sultanate led by Nur ibn Mujahid.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 7. Susenyos (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: In 1622, Emperor Susenyos officially declared Catholicism the state religion of Ethiopia, leading to massive rebellions and his eventual abdication.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 8. Mintewab (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Empress Mentewab was a highly influential figure who heavily dominated Gondarine politics from the reign of her husband Bakaffa up through the reigns of her son Iyasu II and grandson Iyoas.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 9. Wubit Amito (2015)

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: Wubit was a Wollo Oromo noblewoman who married Emperor Iyasu II. Her presence in the court introduced the Yejju/Wollo Oromo as a major power bloc in Gondar, contesting Empress Mentewab's influence.

hist_2015.subject: History

options.text: A. Officially announced Catholicism was a state religion in Ethiopia.
B. A dominant woman in Gonderine court politics from 1728 to 1768.
C. The first Christian monarch who agreed to secretly convert into Catholicism.
D. The wife of Iyasu II and she represents the growing power of Wollo Oromo in Gonderine court.
E. His death marked the onset of the period of Zemene Mesafint.
F. A mother and regent of Libne Dingil played major role in the medieval politics of Christian kingdom.
G. A Queen mother, who advised Gelawdewos to prepare and march to Weyna-Dega.
H. Wife of Imam Ahmed and encouraged her husband to avenge the death of her father.
I. Defeated by Ahmed Gragn at Shimbera Kure in 1529.
J. In 1559 killed by sultanate of Adal led by Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid.

hist_2015.explanation: The assassination of Emperor Iyoas I in 1769 by Ras Mikael Sehul effectively collapsed the central authority of the Gondarine monarchs, ushering in the decentralized Era of the Princes (Zemene Mesafint).

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 1. The main cause for the decline of Aksumite kingdom was ___ (2015)

options.text: A. Rebellion of Beja and Agaw peoples
C. Losses of control over the Red Sea trade
D. Strong opposition from the church which considered the as illegitimate rulers

hist_2015.explanation: The primary cause for the decline of the Aksumite Kingdom was the loss of control over the lucrative Red Sea trade routes following the expansion of the Arab Islamic empire in the 7th century, cutting Aksum off from its major economic lifeline.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 2. Which one is FALSE about Da'amat? (2015)

options.text: A. Its rulers used a title called Mukarib
B. It was the immediate precursor of the Aksumite empire
C. Inscriptions of its ruler written in Ge'ez language indicated its strong relation with Egypt
D. They have strong relation with South Arabia

hist_2015.explanation: Option C is false because the inscriptions found from the Da'amat period were written in Epigraphic South Arabian (Sabaean), not Ge'ez, and their strongest cultural and political relations were with South Arabia (Saba), not Egypt.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 3. The founder of the Zagwe kingdom was ___ (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Mara Takla Haymanot (Mera Teklehaimanot) overthrew the last Aksumite king (Dil Na'od) and founded the Zagwe dynasty in the 12th century.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 4. A kingdom in Gibe region which real power rested with the council (Mikretcho) (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: In the Kingdom of Ennarea (Enarya), real political power was held by a powerful state council known as the Mikretcho, which could even decide on the appointment or deposition of the king.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 5. The earliest Muslim Sultanates in Ethiopia was ___ (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The Sultanate of Shewa (established by the Makhzumi dynasty around 896 AD) is considered the earliest recorded Muslim state in Ethiopia.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 6. The main gateway of Islam in to Ethiopia and the Horn was ___ (2015)

options.text: A. Dahlak Island in the Red Sea
B. Zaila in the Gulf of Aden
C. Mogadishu in the Indian Ocean
D. Massawa in the Red Sea area

hist_2015.explanation: Zeila (Zaila) on the Gulf of Aden served as the primary commercial and religious gateway for the introduction of Islam into the interior of the Horn of Africa and the Ethiopian highlands.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 7. Aksumite and Zagwe rulers were similar in that both of them had ___ (2015)

options.text: D. Trading through the port of Adulis

hist_2015.explanation: Both the Aksumite and Zagwe dynasties adhered to the tradition established in the 4th century of bringing their religious head, the Abuna (Bishop), from the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria in Egypt.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 8. Which religious movement emphasized on poverty, absolute self-subsistence, equality and independence from secular authorities? (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The Estifanosites (followers of Abba Estifanos) were a 15th-century monastic reform movement that strictly emphasized apostolic poverty, self-reliance, and notably refused to bow to secular authorities, which brought them into severe conflict with Emperor Zara Yaqob.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 9. The main base for the relationship between Christian Kingdom and Sultan of Egypt was ___ (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Religion was the primary linkage; Ethiopian kings depended on Egypt for the appointment of the Abuna, while the Egyptian Sultans sought Ethiopian tolerance of Muslims and feared the Ethiopian monarchs' capability to divert the flow of the Nile.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 10. The document that played a major role in the restoration of 'Solomonic dynasty' was: (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The Kebra Nagast (Glory of Kings) served as the foundational ideological text that legitimized the "restored" Solomonic dynasty by asserting their direct descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 11. The event that strengthened the relation between the Christian Kingdom and Christian Europe in the 15th century was: (2015)

options.text: A. The arrival of the Ottoman Turkey in Ethiopia.
B. The revival of relations between the Christian Kingdom and Sultans of Egypt.
C. The rivalry between the Christian Kingdom and Muslim Sultanates.
D. The religious reforms of Emperor Zara-Yaqob

hist_2015.explanation: The increasing geopolitical and economic rivalry with the expanding Muslim Sultanates in the Horn prompted Ethiopian monarchs to seek technical assistance and anti-Muslim military alliances with Christian European nations.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 12. The medieval royal prison was established at: (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Amba Gishen was established as a highly secure mountaintop royal prison where male heirs to the throne were confined to prevent succession disputes and civil wars.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 13. The two medieval market centres in Amhara were: (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: During the medieval period, Wez-Gebeya and Dukkar functioned as critical trading and market centers located in the central Amhara region of the Christian kingdom.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 14. Among the following one is not correct about the Ethio-European relations in the 15th C? (2015)

options.text: A. Admiration and request of Ethiopian monarchs for European technical assistance.
B. Europeans demand for a Christian allies against the Muslims.
C. Exchange of delegations and missions between Ethiopia and Europe.
D. European colonial interest in Ethiopia.

hist_2015.explanation: European relations with Ethiopia in the 15th century were based on mutual religious solidarity and strategic alliance against Islamic expansion. Direct European colonial interest and aggression did not emerge until much later, in the 19th century.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 15. In the medieval Ethiopia the renowned philosophical work belongs to: (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The most renowned philosophical work in Ethiopian history is the Hatata, written by the 17th-century rationalist philosopher Zera Yacob (Zara Ya'iqob). Though chronologically post-medieval, he is conventionally the correct answer when identifying Ethiopia's premier historical philosopher.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 16. The Period of Zemene Mesafint in Ethiopian history is marked by all the following except: (2015)

options.text: A. the decline of the power of kings
B. the rise of powerful regional lords
C. the complete abolition of the central government
D. the domination of the Yeju lords over the lords in Northern Ethiopia

hist_2015.explanation: While the central government was severely weakened and the emperors became mere puppets of the regional lords, the institution of the monarchy itself was never completely abolished during the Zemene Mesafint.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 17. Why did emperor Susenyos abdicate his throne in favor of his son, Fasiladas in 1632? (2015)

options.text: A. The existing controversies and rebellions against his religious policy
B. The conflict between Susenyos and the Jesuits
C. His attempt to continue power transfer along the "Solomonic" lines
D. His attempt to exercise democracy in Ethiopia

hist_2015.explanation: Emperor Susenyos abdicated in 1632 because his attempt to impose Catholicism as the state religion sparked massive, bloody civil wars and nationwide rebellions that made his continued rule untenable.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 18. Which one of the following is not true about the consequences of the war of Ahmad Gragn? (2015)

options.text: A. The Christian kingdom emerged stronger than ever before
B. An easy infiltration and success of the Oromos in their population movement.
C. The weakening of the Muslim sultanate of Adal
D. cultural interaction among the peoples of Ethiopia

hist_2015.explanation: Option A is false. Both the Christian Kingdom and the Adal Sultanate emerged severely exhausted and weakened from decades of devastating warfare, making them highly vulnerable to the subsequent Oromo migrations.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 19. The Gada system in the Oromo society is characterized by all the following features except: (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: The Gada system operates on a strict cyclical basis where age sets rotate through power every eight years. Leaders serve only for their designated term, fundamentally opposing any concept of lifetime leadership.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 20. Which one of the following Gada grades consists of leaders of the Gada government? (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: In the Oromo Gada system, the 'Luba' grade is the ruling class consisting of men in their prime (traditionally ages 40-48) who hold the political and administrative leadership of the society.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 21. The Jesuit mission which arrived in Ethiopia in 1557 led by Andre de Ovideo aimed at: (2015)

options.text: A. Signing bilateral trade agreement with the Christian kingdom
B. Taking side with the Christians in the war against the Muslims
C. Expand Catholicism contrary to Monophysite theology of Ethiopian Orthodox Church
D. Competing with the Ottomans in the Red Sea trade

hist_2015.explanation: Bishop Andrés de Oviedo and his Jesuit mission were dispatched to Ethiopia with the primary goal of convincing the Ethiopian Emperor to reject the native Monophysite (Miaphysite) theology and convert the country to Roman Catholicism.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 22. Who was invited to come to Gondar from Tigray by Empress Mintewab to counter the growing power of the Wollo Oromo in the royal court? (2015)
hist_2015.explanation: Empress Mentewab invited the powerful warlord Ras Mikael Sehul of Tigray to Gondar in 1768 to help her suppress the growing influence of the Wollo Oromo nobility, a move that catastrophically backfired when he seized power himself.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 1. List the main features of Zemene Mesafint 1769-1855? (2015)
hist_2015.answer: The main features include the severe decline of the central monarch's power (becoming mere puppets in Gondar), the rise of powerful regional warlords (Rases) constantly warring for dominance, the political domination of the Yejju dynasty, severe economic decline and disruption of trade due to instability, and intense religious and doctrinal controversies within the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
hist_2015.explanation: Zemene Mesafint (the Era of the Princes) is defined by its intense political fragmentation. Understanding its features requires recognizing the collapse of central authority in favor of regional militarism, alongside simultaneous religious schisms which further fractured Ethiopian unity.

hist_2015.subject: History
hist_2015.text: 2. Write the consequences of the Oromo population movement of the 16th C. (2015)
hist_2015.answer: The consequences included massive demographic shifts as Oromos settled across vast new territories in Ethiopia; deep cultural and linguistic assimilation through inclusive institutions like Gudifacha and Mogasa; major alterations in regional political dynamics as Oromo groups integrated into state politics; and complex religious interactions, with many adopting Christianity or Islam while maintaining aspects of their traditional Gada beliefs.
hist_2015.explanation: The 16th-century Oromo expansion permanently altered the demographic and political map of Ethiopia. A comprehensive answer highlights not just geographical expansion, but the mechanisms of social assimilation (Mogasa/Gudifacha) that integrated conquered peoples into Oromo society, establishing modern Ethiopian ethnolinguistic demographics.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 1. Read the statement and write TRUE if correct, FALSE if wrong: The Somalis had an indigenous governance system known as Makabanto. (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The Makabanto was an indigenous governance and conflict resolution system belonging to the Afar people. The Somali people traditionally utilized a different egalitarian system governed by customary law known as Xeer, overseen by clan elders.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 2. Read the statement and write TRUE if correct, FALSE if wrong: An epitome of Emperor Yohannes IV's willingness to give regional lords a great deal of autonomy was his recognition of Adal Tessema as Negus Teklehaymanot of Gojjam and Keffa. (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Unlike his predecessor Tewodros II who sought strict centralization, Emperor Yohannes IV adopted a decentralized approach. He recognized powerful regional lords as long as they acknowledged him as Emperor. Crowning Ras Adal Tessema as Negus (King) of Gojjam (and nominally Keffa) in 1881 is a prime historical example of this policy.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 3. Read the statement and write TRUE if correct, FALSE if wrong: Zara-Yaqob had made peace with the House of Deqiqe Estifanos but not with Ewostatewos. (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Emperor Zara Yaqob fiercely persecuted the Deqiqe Estifanos (Stephanites) for their refusal to prostrate to the cross or the Virgin Mary. Conversely, he actively sought and achieved reconciliation with the Ewostatians regarding the Sabbath controversy at the Council of Debre Mitmaq in 1450.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 4. Read the statement and write TRUE if correct, FALSE if wrong: In mid-1870s the Western Gurage peacefully submitted to Menilek because of their religious affinity and geographical proximity to Shewa. (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: It was the Northern Gurage, specifically the Kistane, who submitted peacefully to Menelik's forces, largely due to their shared Orthodox Christian faith and the desire for protection against neighboring Oromo groups. The Western Gurage fiercely resisted Shewan expansion.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 5. Read the statement and write TRUE if correct, FALSE if wrong: Moggasa was a system of adopting non-Oromos commonly known as Oromsu. (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Moggasa was a vital socio-political institution of the Oromo that allowed for the mass adoption and assimilation of non-Oromo individuals and entire communities into the Oromo clan structure, a process often referred to as Oromization or Oromsu.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 6. Read the statement and write TRUE if correct, FALSE if wrong: The Sheikhdoms of Assosa/Aqoldi, Bela-Shangul, Khomosha and Guba were founded by Muslim leaders of Sudanese origin. (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The sheikhdoms in the western borderlands emerged in the late 19th century and were heavily influenced by Islamic penetration from the Mahdist state. They were established by leaders who had strong ethnic and religious ties to the neighboring Sudanese Muslim populations.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 7. Read the statement and write TRUE if correct, FALSE if wrong: The territorial expansion during the medieval period led to the spread of Christianity. (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: During the medieval era, particularly under Solomonic kings like Amda Seyon and Zara Yaqob, territorial conquest of adjacent pagan and Muslim areas was systematically followed by state-sponsored evangelization and the establishment of churches to consolidate imperial control.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 8. Match the explanation with the corresponding battlefield: Fought between Kasa Hailu of Quara and Egyptian forces in 1848 (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: In 1848, Kasa Hailu (the future Emperor Tewodros II) led his forces against an Egyptian garrison at Dabarki. He suffered a heavy defeat due to the Egyptians' superior firearms and discipline, a lesson that profoundly influenced his later military reforms.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 9. Match the explanation with the corresponding battlefield: Fought between Emperor Yohannes IV and the Mahdists in 1889 (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The Battle of Metemma (or Gallabat) took place in March 1889. Despite initially routing the Sudanese Mahdist forces, Emperor Yohannes IV was mortally wounded, leading to the collapse of the Ethiopian army and a catastrophic defeat.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 10. Match the explanation with the corresponding battlefield: Fought between Emperor Menelik II and Italian forces in 1896 (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The Battle of Adwa, fought on March 1, 1896, resulted in a decisive victory for Emperor Menelik II's forces against the invading Italian colonial army, successfully preserving Ethiopia's independence.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 11. Match the explanation with the corresponding battlefield: Fought between Emperor Tewodros II and British forces in 1868 (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The Battle of Maqdela (1868) marked the climax of the British expedition led by Robert Napier. Tewodros II's forces were defeated at Aroge, and as the British stormed the fortress of Maqdela, the Emperor committed suicide rather than be captured.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 12. Match the explanation with the corresponding battlefield: Fought between Emperor Yohannes IV and Egyptian forces in 1875 (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: In November 1875, Emperor Yohannes IV ambushed and completely annihilated a well-equipped Egyptian expeditionary force led by the Danish mercenary Colonel Arendrup at the Battle of Gundet.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 13. Match the explanation with the corresponding battlefield: Fought between Emperor Tekle-Giorgis II and Kasa Mircha of Tigray in July 1871 (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: At the Battle of Assam (near Adwa) in 1871, Kasa Mircha decisively defeated Emperor Tekle Giyorgis II. Kasa's victory was largely due to the modern firearms he had acquired from the British Napier expedition, paving his way to be crowned Yohannes IV.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 14. Match the explanation with the corresponding battlefield: Fought between Emperor Yohannes IV and Italian forces in 1887 (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: In January 1887, Ethiopian forces under the command of Ras Alula Engida intercepted and massacred an Italian column attempting to reinforce their garrison at Saati. This encounter is known as the Battle of Dogali.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 15. The first Solomonic king who embarked a policy of wider and rapid territorial expansion in medieval period was: (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Emperor Amda Seyon I (r. 1314–1344) is renowned in Ethiopian history as the foundational military leader of the Solomonic Dynasty. He initiated a massive and rapid wave of conquests, subduing powerful Muslim sultanates like Ifat and vastly expanding the borders of the Christian Kingdom.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 16. Among the following one is the consequence of the population movements of the peoples of Afar, Argobba and Somali. (2015)

options.text: A. Forced the Christian Kingdom to shift its political centre
C. Strengthening the military force of Ahmed ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi
D. Restricted the Sultanate of Adal to the walled town of Harar.

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The population pressures and movements of nomadic and semi-nomadic groups in the eastern lowlands provided a vast, motivated manpower pool. Ahmed Gragn successfully channeled these demographic pressures, recruiting heavily from Afar, Somali, and Argobba populations to build the formidable army he used to invade the Christian Kingdom.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 17. All of the following statements have persuasive idea in relation to the Gibe Oromo States EXCEPT: (2015)

options.text: A. They were all monarchical States.
B. They were founded by Abba Dulas who had assumed the title of Moti.
C. All of them were formed in the 19th century at the expense of the Gada System.
D. Long distance trade had nothing to do with the establishment of these states.

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The statement in option D is false, making it the correct answer for the 'EXCEPT' question. Control and taxation of the lucrative long-distance trade routes passing through the Gibe region provided ambitious war leaders (Abba Dulas) with the wealth and firearms necessary to consolidate power, abandon the egalitarian Gada system, and establish centralized monarchies.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 18. Which of the following is NOT the feature of Christian Highland Kingdom in the early medieval period of Ethiopia? (2015)

options.text: C. The beginning of political decay ever in the history of the region

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The early medieval period (following the 1270 Solomonic restoration) was an era of unprecedented strength, rapid expansion, and religious consolidation under powerful monarchs. Political decay and extreme fragmentation characterized the much later Zemene Mesafint (Era of the Princes) in the 18th and 19th centuries.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 19. Which of the following is NOT true about a royal prison of Amba-Gishen? (2015)

options.text: A. All male members of the royal family were confined
B. The prison was guarded by royal families
C. The court dignitaries escorted the designated successor and put him on the throne

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Amba Gishen was heavily fortified and guarded by a dedicated garrison of fiercely loyal, specially appointed soldiers—not by members of the royal family. The royal family members were the inmates kept there to prevent civil wars over succession.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 20. The long distance trade of the 19th Century Ethiopia and the Horn was characterized by: (2015)

options.text: A. uniform use of a single medium of exchange
B. the existence of two main trade lines that linked various territories of Ethiopia and the Horn
C. export of such luxurious commodities as mirrors and ironware
D. export of trade items taken from Northern Ethiopia other than goods from southwest regions

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: 19th-century Ethiopian trade primarily flowed along two major arterial routes: a northwestern route crossing Gojjam towards Metemma and Massawa, and an eastern route connecting the wealthy southwestern states (like Keffa and Jimma) through Shewa to Harar and the coastal ports.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 21. The immediate cause of the Zemene Mesafint was: (2015)

options.text: A. Religious dispute within the Ethiopian Orthodox church
B. Power struggle between the Quara and Wollo political groups
C. The assassination of Iyoas by Ras Michael Sehul
D. The death of Iyasu I

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The assassination of Emperor Iyoas I in 1769 by Ras Mikael Sehul, the powerful governor of Tigray, shattered the aura of imperial invincibility. This act of regicide marked the definitive collapse of central authority and ushered in the Zemene Mesafint, where regional warlords held true power.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 22. Tewodros II King of Kings of Ethiopia is remembered in the history pages of the country for: (2015)

options.text: A. the appointment of the first foreign consul who served as his representative in London
B. his attempt to create a strong central government by appointing individuals who would be totally accountable to him
C. attempt to introduce a decentralized system of administration, permitting regional rulers to exercise a great deal of autonomy.
D. a campaign to convert Muslims and adherents of other religions into Orthodox Christianity

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Emperor Tewodros II's paramount historical legacy is his violent but determined effort to dismantle the fragmented power structure of the Zemene Mesafint. He attempted to replace hereditary regional warlords with salaried officials directly appointed by and solely loyal to the central crown.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 23. The Anti-Ewostatewos group was led by: (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Aqabe-Se'at Serqe Birhan was an influential conservative cleric within the imperial court who fiercely led the opposition against the Ewostatian movement, demanding that they abandon their observance of the Saturday Sabbath.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 24. Among those powerful kings of Gondar who established a separate living quarter for Muslims at Addis Alem? (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: During a church council convened in 1668, Emperor Yohannes I decreed that Muslims residing in the capital of Gondar must live in a separate designated quarter, physically segregating them from the Christian population. This district became known as Addis Alem.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 25. The first center of Walasma dynasty of Adal was: (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Following the destruction of the Sultanate of Ifat by Emperor Amda Seyon, the surviving members of the Walasma dynasty retreated eastward and founded the Sultanate of Adal. They established their first administrative and military center at Dakar, before it was later moved to Harar in the 16th century.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 26. The intervention of which European power in the conflict between Adal and Christian Kingdom led the war to take an international dimension? (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The 16th-century devastating war between the Christian Kingdom and the Adal Sultanate (under Ahmed Gragn) became an international proxy conflict when Portugal deployed a heavily armed contingent of musketeers to save the Christian Kingdom, while the Ottoman Empire supplied firearms, artillery, and mercenaries to bolster Adal.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 27. Which one of the following modernization reforms was made during the Dual Rule (1916-30)? (2015)

options.text: A. Ethiopia's entry into the League of Nations
B. The prohibition of Quragna System
C. The promulgation of Ethiopia's first constitution
D. The introduction of modern style vaccine against Smallpox to Ethiopia

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The period of Dual Rule saw Empress Zewditu as head of state and Ras Tafari (later Haile Selassie) as regent. Tafari led Ethiopia's successful diplomatic campaign to join the League of Nations in 1923, a critical modernization step cementing the country's international sovereignty.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 28. In 1841, the British envoy named Captain Corn Wallis Harris had signed the Treaty of Friendship and commerce with: (2015)

options.text: A. Ras Wolde Selassie of Tigray
B. Ras Ali Alula of the Yejju Dynasty
C. Negus Sahle Selassie of Shewa

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: During the Zemene Mesafint, regional rulers conducted independent foreign policies. Captain Cornwallis Harris led a British diplomatic mission to the powerful, independent kingdom of Shewa and successfully signed a commercial treaty with its ruler, Negus Sahle Selassie, in 1841.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 29. Which one of the following Catholic missionary leading members did NOT play key role in the efforts to evangelize Ethiopia? (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Joao Bermudez, Pedro Paez, and Alfonso Mendez were all prominent clerics deeply involved in aggressive Portuguese Jesuit efforts to convert Ethiopia to Catholicism. Christopher da Gama, by contrast, was a military commander sent strictly to lead the 400 Portuguese musketeers in battle against Ahmed Gragn.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 30. The relationship between the Christian Kingdom and Egypt in early medieval period was NOT highly influenced by: (2015)

options.text: A. the existence of Muslim minorities in Ethiopia
D. the existence of Coptic Church in Egypt

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Early medieval relations were dominated by ideological and resource conflicts—Ethiopian kings threatened to dam the Nile if Mamluk Egypt persecuted its Coptic Christians, while Egypt leveraged its control over the appointment of the Ethiopian Abun. Because the two states were separated by vast tracts of desert and pastoralist societies, direct territorial border disputes were not a central factor during this era.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 31. How did the major foreign powers of the world recognize Ethiopia's independence after the historic Battle of Adwa? (2015)

options.text: A. By providing a huge sum of money which could enable Ethiopia recover from the ruins of the battle
B. By facilitating the restoration of Messewa to Ethiopia from the hands of Italy
C. By opening their legations in Addis Ababa
D. By training and equipping Ethiopia's military in modern ways

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Ethiopia's stunning victory over Italy at Adwa compelled European colonial powers to treat the nation as an equal on the global stage. They demonstrated formal recognition of its sovereignty by dispatching envoys and establishing permanent diplomatic missions (legations) in the capital, Addis Ababa.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 32. What was the main inquiry of Ewostatians movement during the 14th and 15th Centuries? (2015)

options.text: A. The veneration of Saint Mary
D. The veneration of the king and religious icons

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Founded by Ewostatewos, this influential monastic movement caused deep divisions within the Ethiopian Orthodox Church by strictly insisting on the observance of the biblical Sabbath (Saturday) in addition to Sunday, challenging prevailing church doctrine.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 33. Which one of the following is a persuasive idea about the Treaty of Neutrality of 1887? (2015)

options.text: A. It was signed between Negus Tekle Haymanot and Italians in a bid to isolate Yohannes IV.
B. It was signed after Italian forces were defeated by Ras Alula's army at the Battle of Dogali.
C. It was a treaty with which Menelik of Shewa expressed his allegiance to Emperor Yohannes IV.
D. It was the treaty which enabled Rubatino Company of Italy to buy the Port of Assab.

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Following the devastating Italian defeat at Dogali in early 1887, Italy desperately needed to prevent a united Ethiopian front. Consequently, in October 1887, Italian diplomat Pietro Antonelli signed a Treaty of Neutrality with King Menelik of Shewa, ensuring Menelik would not assist Emperor Yohannes IV in a potential wider war.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 34. One of the following is NOT a result of long-distance trade in the medieval Ethiopia. (2015)

options.text: A. cause for the emergence of a number of strong Muslim sultanates
B. major source of conflict between the Christian Kingdom and Muslim sultanates
C. a source of interaction between different ethnic groups and religions
D. the major channel of social disintegration

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Long-distance trade in medieval Ethiopia was a powerful catalyst for state formation, urbanization, and cross-cultural contact. While competition over trade routes did cause state-level wars, the trade networks themselves facilitated interaction and economic integration, rather than causing broad societal disintegration.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 35. Which one of the following does NOT describe Emperor Susenyos? He: (2015)

options.text: A. was converted to Catholicism and announced it to be state religion in 1622
B. integrated the Oromo with the forces of the central government
C. established more than one royal camps/ketamas in Lake Tana region
D. was brutally killed by his own people

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Emperor Susenyos voluntarily abdicated the throne in 1632 in favor of his son Fasilides after realizing that his attempt to force Catholicism upon his subjects had sparked a devastating civil war. He retired and died of natural causes (illness) shortly after, rather than being murdered.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 36. One of the following CAN NOT be taken as the common feature of Peoples and States in Central, South, Southeast and West parts of Ethiopia in early 16th and end of 18th centuries. (2015)

options.text: A. Their land is known for its less fertility and harsh climate.
B. All these had traditional system of governance developed over the centuries.
C. They had their own leaders.
D. They were constantly at move and contacted to other ethnic groups, example, the Oromos.

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The southern and southwestern regions of Ethiopia (such as Ennarea, Keffa, and the Gibe river basin) are historically famous for their lush, highly fertile environments and favorable climates, which supported dense populations and abundant cash crops like coffee, completely contradicting option A.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 37. What event immediately sparked off the second phase patriotic resistance movement in 1937? (2015)

options.text: A. Wal Wal Incident and resulting military skirmishes between Ethiopian and Italian troops
B. Merciless killing of thousands of innocent Ethiopians after the abortive attempt to kill Graziani
C. The assassination of one of the unifying spirits of the movement, Abune Petros
D. The return of Emperor Haile Selassie I from his exile to Ethiopia

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Following a failed grenade attack on the Italian Viceroy Rodolfo Graziani in February 1937, Italian fascists unleashed a campaign of indiscriminate slaughter in Addis Ababa known as Yekatit 12. This brutal massacre deeply outraged the Ethiopian populace and served as the primary catalyst for the widespread, intensified second phase of the guerrilla resistance (the Arbegnoch movement).

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 38. The restoration of Solomonic Dynasty in Ethiopian history refers: (2015)

options.text: A. The period between the emergence of Zagwe dynasty to 1500
B. Aksumite period, Zagwe dynasty and Medieval period
C. The restoration of King Solomon of Israel and Queen Sheba's lineage after the fall of Zagwe dynasty
D. The period between King Menelik I to Zagwe Dynasty

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: When Yekuno Amlak overthrew the last Zagwe king in 1270, he legitimized his usurpation by claiming direct patrilineal descent from the ancient Aksumite kings, who according to the Kebra Nagast were the descendants of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Thus, his ascension is historically referred to as the 'Restoration' of the Solomonic line.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 39. Gondar served as a permanent capital for about one hundred fifty years and achieved cityhood because: (2015)

options.text: A. The city had an estimated 60,000-70,000 population.
B. The city became residence of foreign communities like Indians, Greeks and Armenians.
C. Kings built significant secular buildings like castles, bridges, residences, bath, library, towers.

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Gondar ended the era of roving capitals by offering a stable urban environment. Its transformation into a true city was characterized by its massive population growth, its cosmopolitan demographics driven by merchant communities, and the monumental architectural legacy of the Fasil Ghebbi complex built by successive emperors.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 40. The Socio-economic reforms of Emperor Tewodros II can be exemplified by his: (2015)

options.text: A. introduction of a privileged army contingent called Kebur Zebegna
B. attempt at the centralization of power at the expense of the centrifugal forces
C. official abandonment of a criminal detection system named Leba Shay
D. attempt to put an end to the slave trade

hist_UoG_2015.explanation: While Tewodros II is famous for his political centralization (option B), his socio-economic reforms included bold edicts attempting to abolish the lucrative slave trade and disrupt local slave markets. (Note: The Kebur Zebegna was created later under Haile Selassie, and the Leba Shay system was abolished during Zewditu's reign).

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 41. List out the cause and consequences of the Oromo Population Movement and expansion. (2 Points) (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.answer: Causes included intense demographic pressure as a growing human and cattle population outstripped the resources of their original homeland, combined with ecological factors like drought. Consequences included the rapid spread of the Oromo across large swathes of Ethiopia, the integration of indigenous populations into Oromo society through the Moggasa assimilation system, and the severe weakening of both the Christian Kingdom and Muslim Sultanates due to perpetual warfare.
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: The 16th-century Oromo expansion was driven by a combination of environmental push factors and the organizational strength of the Gadaa system. Its historical consequences were monumental, permanently altering the ethno-linguistic landscape of the Horn of Africa and shifting the balance of power away from the established states.

hist_UoG_2015.subject: History
hist_UoG_2015.text: 42. Enumerate the main features of Emperor Tewodros II's military reforms (4 points). (2015)
hist_UoG_2015.answer: 1) The creation of a national, centrally salaried standing army to stop troops from violently plundering the peasantry. 2) The introduction of modern military discipline, clear hierarchical ranks, and uniform structures. 3) The ambitious attempt to establish an indigenous arms manufacturing industry, notably conscripting European missionaries at Gafat to cast cannons and mortars (like the famous 'Sebastopol'). 4) The systematic dismantling of regional warlords' private armies to concentrate all military force under the Emperor's direct command.
hist_UoG_2015.explanation: Tewodros recognized that to end the Zemene Mesafint and defend against foreign incursions, he needed a modern military. His reforms targeted the root causes of internal instability—unpaid, undisciplined regional militias—by attempting to forge a disciplined, well-equipped, and centrally loyal national force.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 1. The external contact of Ethiopia was limited only to the Christian Europe. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: Ethiopia maintained extensive external contacts well beyond Christian Europe, particularly with the Middle East, Egypt, Yemen, and various Islamic states, driven by trade, religious ties, and diplomacy.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 2. The conflicts between the Christian kingdom and Adal sultanate contributed for cultural intermixing of various linguistic and religious groups in Ethiopia and the Horn. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The series of conflicts and subsequent population movements, especially during the 16th century, led to significant cultural, linguistic, and religious intermixing among the peoples of the Ethiopian region.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 3. During the reign of Emir Nur Mujahid, Harar became a walled City. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: Emir Nur ibn Mujahid built the protective wall around Harar, known as the Jugol, in the 1560s to defend the city against Oromo expansion and other threats.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 4. Administrative organization of Ari people was based on highly centralized monarchy. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The traditional administrative organization of the Ari people was decentralized, structured around independent chiefdoms (such as Bako, Shangama, etc.) rather than a single highly centralized monarchy.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 5. The Medieval Kingdom of Shawa was founded during the reign of Menelik II. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The Medieval Kingdom of Shewa (such as the Makhzumite or Walasma states) existed centuries before Menelik II. Menelik II was the king of the later Shewan kingdom in the 19th century before becoming Emperor of all Ethiopia.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 6. Emperor Yohannes IV attempted to introduce a decentralized system of administration more than Emperor Tewodros II. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: Unlike Tewodros II, who attempted strict and uncompromising centralization, Yohannes IV adopted a more pragmatic, decentralized approach, granting regional lords (like Menelik of Shewa and Tekle Haymanot of Gojjam) significant autonomy provided they recognized his supreme authority.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 7. In the 17th C, Jesuit missionaries promoted Catholicism with some elements of teaching that contradicted with the doctrine of the Orthodox Church in Ethiopia and the Horn. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: Jesuit missionaries, notably Afonso Mendes, aggressively promoted Catholicism and attempted to suppress Orthodox practices (like circumcision and Saturday Sabbath), leading to widespread rebellion and Emperor Susenyos's eventual abdication.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 8. The long distance trade of the 19th century had no negative impact on the Ethiopian society. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The long-distance trade of the 19th century had severe negative impacts, most notably the widespread expansion of the slave trade, which devastated many local communities.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 9. The military victories of Ethiopia over Egypt liberated all occupied territories in the north. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: While Ethiopia won decisive battles against Egypt (such as Gundet and Gura), they did not liberate all occupied territories; regions like Bogos remained contested and eventually fell under Italian control.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 10. The victory of Adwa (1896) has been nothing to do with the African Nationalism. (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The Battle of Adwa was a seminal event that deeply inspired African Nationalism and the global Pan-African movement by demonstrating that an African nation could successfully defeat a European colonial power.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 11. It claims that Ethiopian ruling class descended from Israel (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The Kebra Nagast (Glory of the Kings) is the foundational text that established the ideological basis for the Solomonic dynasty, claiming their descent from the biblical King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 12. It retreated to Harar in 14th century and then abandoned it to Awsa in 1577 (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The Walasma dynasty ruled the Sultanate of Ifat and later the Sultanate of Adal. Due to Christian military pressure and Oromo expansion, they relocated their center to Harar and eventually to Awsa in the late 16th century.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 13. An age-set organization of the Sidama society (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The Luwa system is the traditional age-set organizational structure of the Sidama people, functioning similarly to the Gadaa system of the Oromo.

hist_Hawassa_2015.subject: History
hist_Hawassa_2015.text: 14. Its Tato was assisted by a council of seven advisors called Mikrecho (2015)
hist_Hawassa_2015.explanation: The Minjo dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Kafa. The king, bearing the title 'Tato', was assisted by a powerful council of state known as the Mikrecho.
